*"Virtually all beginners initially estimate the duration of every meteor to be one or two seconds, which is impossible. The average meteor duration is more like 0.4 second. Following are durations and likely visual impressions. A streak or flash with no moving body visible is 0.2 to 0.3 second, which constitutes the majority of meteors. Rather rare is 0.1 second, only a few per year at most. The moving body may be visible at 0.4 second, and quite likely is at 0.5 second. At 0.7 second the meteor is rather prolonged and easy to see; definitely so at 1.0 second. Exceptions would be meteors with very long paths. The eye can comfortably follow a meteor lasting longer than 1.0 second, allowing time for brief study of the object.

There is no set upper duration for meteors. Experienced observers have reported an occasional meteor at ten seconds. Beyond perhaps five seconds, however, the possibility of re-entering space junk arises. The possibility must be considered in conjunction with path length and low altitude of a major shower radiant. A shower meteor skimming the top of the atmosphere might take 5 or more seconds to traverse 90 degrees or more, much too fast for a re-entry."*
